h1: From homebrewer to assistant brewer: a first-year plan
title: From Homebrewer to Assistant Brewer | Craft Beer School
desc: A first-year plan for a homebrewer who wants an assistant brewer job: what changes at scale, skills to build and how to get hired.
teaser: Good home beer is a start. Commercial brewing asks for different habits. Here is a plan for the first year.
standfirst: Moving from a 20 L (5 US gal) kettle to a commercial brewhouse changes what matters. This guide sets out twelve months of preparation and early work.
sections:
A homebrewer makes beer that tastes good. An assistant brewer makes the same beer every time, safely, to a schedule, with records. Volumes are larger, so mistakes cost more. A tank of 1,000 L (264 US gal) that goes wrong cannot be tipped down the sink without a conversation about money.

Cleaning takes up more hours than brewing. Heavy lifting, hot liquid and chemicals become daily matters. Cold chain, packaging lines and excise or duty paperwork enter the picture. Expect to learn all of it.

One more habit changes: you stop tinkering mid-batch. A recipe at commercial scale is a procedure. The aim is to follow it the same way each time. Variation is what you track, not what you enjoy.
Months one to three: close the gaps

List what you have never done at home: cleaning in place, yeast propagation, measuring dissolved oxygen, working with a pump, filling kegs. Read about each. Take a structured course if your knowledge has holes in water chemistry or fermentation control. Brewing Fundamentals covers the process in four weeks of live classes.

Refine your tasting. Join a tasting panel, practise with off-flavour kits and read beer off-flavours. Employers notice a candidate who can name diacetyl.

Measure your own home process too. Record mash pH, pre-boil gravity and the volume you actually collect. If you can predict your numbers before you brew, you have the habit a brewhouse wants.
Months four to six: get inside a brewery

Volunteer or take a part-time packaging or taproom job. Watch the daily rhythm. Ask to be shown the brew sheet and the cleaning schedule. Offer to do the dull jobs well. Bring a notebook. Write down every measurement and every correction.

Look at starting in a taproom to learn the trade if a brewery job is not yet open.

Shadow a full cycle if you can: brew day, fermentation checks, transfer, packaging. Ask what the brewer is looking at when they walk past a fermenter.
Months seven to nine: apply for assistant roles

A good application is short and specific. List the beers you have brewed, the volumes, the equipment, any competition results and your relevant courses. Add a line on what you want to learn. Ask a brewer you volunteered with for a reference.

In an interview, expect questions on sanitation, mash temperature and how you would deal with a stuck fermentation. Be honest about gaps. A candidate who says I have not run a plate heat exchanger, but I know why it needs cleaning, wins trust.

Do not criticise a brewery's beer in an interview. Ask what they are proud of and what they would like to improve.
Months ten to twelve: be useful and keep a log

In your first months as assistant, learn the brewery's routine before you suggest changes. Keep a log of what you were taught and what went wrong. Track simple numbers: brew-day length, volume into the fermenter, loss at packaging, days from yeast pitch to packaging. A brewer who measures becomes valuable.

Ask to take on a defined job, such as the daily gravity checks or the yeast log. Owning a small task builds trust faster than offering opinions.

Respect hot liquid, caustic cleaners, carbon dioxide and heavy lifting. Never enter a tank without the confined space procedure that your country or employer sets. Report near misses. A brewery that is safe is a brewery that keeps its staff.

Taste responsibly at work. Spit when sampling many beers and drink water. Never drive after tasting.

Learn where the eyewash station and the emergency stop are on day one. Ask before you operate any machine you have not been shown.

After a year, decide what you want next: head brewer, quality, packaging, a specialist style. Our Style Specialisation and Advanced Brewing Science courses go deeper once you have the basics. We do not quote salaries or promise promotion; both depend on the brewery and the country.

If you are ready to start the structured part of this plan, Brewing Fundamentals is where it begins. Save your seat and start the assignments while you volunteer.
faqs: How big is the step from home to commercial?
Large in discipline and scale, smaller in the core biology. The skills that change are cleaning, record keeping and working to a schedule.
Do I need a degree to become an assistant brewer?
Not at most breweries, although it helps for larger companies and lab roles.
Should I mention my homebrew competition results?
Yes, briefly, together with the batch sizes and equipment you have used.
How soon can I become head brewer?
It depends on the brewery and your results. Do not rush the basics.
